title: RAHAB IS CALLED A PROSTITUTE—And Hebrews Still Lists Her Among Examples of Faith
paragraphs: RAHAB IS CALLED A PROSTITUTE—And Hebrews Still Lists Her Among Examples of Faith
What if the part of your story you are most ashamed of is the very place where Jesus intends to show the world what grace can do?
There is something almost uncomfortable about the way the Bible introduces Rahab.
Scripture does not soften it.
It does not clean up her résumé before allowing her onto the pages of sacred history.
It does not introduce her as “Rahab, the courageous woman.”
Not first.
It does not call her “Rahab, the woman of extraordinary faith.”
Not first.
It does not call her “Rahab, an ancestor in the line that would lead to Jesus Christ.”
Not first.
Joshua introduces her with words that generations would remember:
אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה — ishah zonah.
A woman.
A prostitute.
Joshua 2:1 identifies her as “a prostitute whose name was Rahab.”
And centuries later, when the writer of Hebrews gathers some of the great examples of faith from Israel’s history, something astonishing happens.
Her past is still mentioned.
Her faith is mentioned louder.
Hebrews 11:31 begins:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη — Pistei Rhaab hē pornē.
“By faith Rahab the prostitute…”
Read that again.
By faith.
Not by reputation.
Not by respectability.
Not because she had lived a spotless life.
Not because her past had somehow vanished from history.
By faith.
And maybe that is exactly why someone reading this right now needs Rahab’s story.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing that the ugliest word attached to your past has become the permanent definition of your future.
Addict.
Adulterer.
Divorced.
Abandoned.
Abuser.
Abused.
Liar.
Failure.
Prisoner.
Unfaithful.
Unwanted.
Impure.
Hypocrite.
Backslider.
Maybe nobody says the word anymore.
But you still hear it.
Sometimes when the room becomes quiet.
Sometimes when you pray.
Sometimes when someone talks about holiness and something inside you whispers, If they only knew.
Sometimes you walk into church carrying a Bible while carrying a secret courtroom inside your head.
The prosecution never rests.
The evidence keeps replaying.
The witnesses are your memories.
And every night your shame rises to announce the same verdict:
This is who you are.
Then Rahab walks into Hebrews 11.
And everything gets complicated.
Because Hebrews 11 is the famous chapter of faith.
Abel is there.
Enoch is there.
Noah is there.
Abraham is there.
Sarah is there.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Joseph.
Moses.
And then…
Rahab.
The prostitute.
The Holy Spirit did not accidentally allow her name onto the page.
Her inclusion is not an embarrassing footnote in the biblical story.
It is a declaration about the astonishing reach of grace and the reality of faith.
Rahab lived in Jericho.
Joshua 2 tells us that Israel was approaching the land God had promised. Joshua sent two spies secretly to inspect Jericho, and they entered Rahab’s house.
The king of Jericho discovered that Israelite men had entered the city and sent orders demanding that Rahab surrender them.
She did not.
She hid them.
And then this Canaanite woman said something remarkable.
“I know that the LORD has given you the land.”
She told the spies that the people of Jericho had heard what the LORD had done—how He had dried up the Red Sea and how Israel’s enemies had fallen before them.
Then Rahab confessed:
“For the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above and on the earth beneath.”
Joshua 2:11.
Do not race past that sentence.
Rahab was living among a people facing judgment, yet she had heard about Israel’s God and responded.
The stories reached Jericho.
Fear filled the city.
But Rahab did something more than tremble.
She acted.
This is why Hebrews does not merely remember Rahab as a woman who was afraid.
It remembers her as a woman who believed.
Biblical faith is not merely agreeing that God exists.
Faith changes what you do because of who you believe God is.
Rahab took a terrifying risk.
She sheltered the spies.
She aligned herself with the God of Israel.
She pleaded for mercy for herself and her family.
And the spies gave her instructions involving a scarlet cord.
When Israel came against Jericho, that cord was to be placed in her window.
Imagine the scene.
A city awaiting destruction.
Walls that looked strong enough to make people feel safe.
Families continuing their lives behind fortified stone.
And hanging from one window…
scarlet.
Rahab had no army.
No religious pedigree.
No Israelite ancestry she could appeal to.
No lifetime of impressive spiritual accomplishments.
She had a promise.
And she trusted it.
That scarlet cord should not be carelessly turned into a direct prophecy that Scripture itself never explicitly calls it.
But it is difficult for a Christian reader not to feel the resonance.
Scarlet.
Deliverance.
Judgment passing while mercy preserves.
And beyond Rahab’s window stands the much greater reality toward which the whole biblical story ultimately moves:
Jesus Christ.
Not a cord hanging from a window…
but the Son of God hanging upon a cross.
There, our salvation does not rest upon our ability to erase our history.
It rests upon Christ’s finished work.
This is where Rahab’s story stops being ancient history and starts becoming painfully personal.
Some of us are still trying to save ourselves by becoming respectable enough that God will finally stop remembering what we did.
But that is not the Gospel.
The Gospel is not God pretending sin was harmless.
The Gospel is God dealing with sin so seriously that His Son went to the cross.
Grace does not say your sin did not matter.
Grace says Jesus Christ is greater.
At Calvary, Jesus bore sin and judgment. Through His death and resurrection, forgiveness and reconciliation with God are proclaimed to sinners who repent and believe.
That means Christianity is not a religion for people who successfully avoided scandal.
It is good news for sinners who need a Savior.
And Rahab needed one.
So do I.
So do you.
That is what makes her presence in Hebrews 11 breathtaking.
Hebrews does not say:
“By faith Rahab the woman with the socially acceptable background…”
It says:
Πίστει Ῥαὰβ ἡ πόρνη.
By faith Rahab the prostitute.
Her past is acknowledged without being allowed to have the final word.
That distinction matters.
Grace does not require us to rewrite history and call darkness light.
Grace tells the truth about what happened…
and then demonstrates that what happened does not have greater authority than God.
Maybe you did wreck things.
Maybe you betrayed somebody.
Maybe you slept with people you wish you had never met.
Maybe pornography has eaten years of your life.
Maybe alcohol became your hiding place.
Maybe you destroyed trust.
Maybe your marriage collapsed partly because of choices you made.
Maybe you walked away from God.
Maybe you have smiled in church while privately living a completely different life.
Maybe the person you were ten years ago still visits you in your dreams.
Repentance does not mean pretending those things never happened.
It means turning from sin toward God.
And grace means your sin does not possess the authority to overrule the mercy God gives in Jesus Christ.
There is an enormous difference between remembering where God rescued you from and continuing to live there.
Rahab did not remain where she was.
Joshua 6 records the fall of Jericho.
The city that appeared untouchable fell.
Rahab and those gathered with her were spared.
Joshua 6:25 says Rahab lived among Israel.
The outsider came inside.
The woman marked by a notorious past was given a future among the covenant people.
But Scripture still was not finished telling her story.
Centuries passed.
Then Matthew opened his Gospel with a genealogy.
Most people hurry through biblical genealogies.
Do not hurry through this one.
Matthew 1:5 says:
“Salmon the father of Boaz by Rahab…”
Rahab.
Boaz.
Boaz became the father of Obed.
Obed became the father of Jesse.
Jesse became the father of David.
And generations later, through this royal line, Matthew brings us to Jesus Christ.
Think about what that means.
The woman whom many people would have reduced to her sexual history appears in the genealogy Matthew uses to introduce the Messiah.
The scandal did not disappear from history.
Grace overwhelmed its authority to define the ending.
This is our theme because it is written all over the Gospel:
Not because scandal is beautiful.
Not because sin should be romanticized.
Not because consequences magically disappear.
But because Jesus rewrites everything.
He takes sinners and makes them saints.
Enemies can be reconciled to God.
The guilty can be forgiven.
The spiritually dead can be made alive.
The lost can be found.
The ashamed can stop hiding.
And the story people thought had reached its final chapter can become evidence that God is still writing.
Rahab even appears again in James 2:25.
James points to her actions in receiving the messengers and sending them out another way.
Hebrews emphasizes her faith.
James emphasizes the action produced by that faith.
There is no contradiction.
There is transformation.
Real faith moves.
Real faith acts.
Real faith changes allegiance.
Rahab did not merely say, “I believe Israel's God is real,” and then hand the spies over to Jericho.
What she believed changed what she risked.
That should confront us.
Because modern Christianity can become frighteningly comfortable with professions of faith that require almost nothing.
We say we believe Jesus is Lord…
but refuse to surrender the secret sin.
We sing about grace…
but refuse to forgive.
We post Bible verses…
but privately feed addictions.
We call Him Savior…
while resisting Him as Lord.
Rahab reminds us that saving faith is not admiration from a distance.
Faith steps out from behind the walls.
Faith entrusts itself to God.
And perhaps your wall is not made of stone.
Perhaps yours is made of shame.
You built it slowly.
One regret at a time.
One secret at a time.
One betrayal at a time.
One night you promised yourself would never happen again.
One browser history you deleted.
One bottle nobody knows about.
One relationship you cannot explain.
One prayer you stopped praying because you became convinced God must be tired of hearing from you.
Brick.
By brick.
By brick.
Until eventually you were living inside your own Jericho.
And Jesus is calling you out.
Not into denial.
Into repentance.
Not into pretending.
Into truth.
Not into self-salvation.
Into grace.
The Gospel does not tell you to make yourself worthy and then approach Christ.
You cannot.
You come because Christ alone is worthy.
Jesus said He came not to call the righteous, but sinners.
The apostolic Gospel announces that Christ died for our sins and rose again.
And the invitation remains astonishingly open:
Repent.
Believe.
Come to Christ.
Stop making peace with the very chains from which He calls you to freedom.
You may have been called many things.
But the question is no longer merely what people called you.
The question is:
Who will you trust now?
Rahab heard what God had done.
She believed.
She acted.
And when Jericho fell, faith had already moved her allegiance beyond those walls.
Maybe your moment is now.
Maybe you have been reading Gospel content for months while keeping Jesus at a safe distance.
Maybe you know Christian vocabulary without knowing surrender.
Maybe you know how to say “Amen” while your heart is exhausted from hiding.
Then stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
He knows the chapter you would delete.
He knows the name.
The bed.
The bottle.
The screen.
The lie.
The betrayal.
The abortion.
The affair.
The bitterness.
The secret.
The relapse.
The years you wasted.
The promises you broke.
And knowing all of it, the Gospel still summons sinners to come to Him in repentance and faith.
Not because sin is insignificant.
Because His grace is astonishing.
If you cannot even find the strength for a long explanation, simply write:
There may be another believer reading the comments who understands exactly what those three words cost you.
And if Jesus has already rescued you from a past that once defined you, tell somebody.
Your testimony may become another person's Jericho moment.
Not because you are the Savior.
You are not.
But because broken people need to see what happens when sinners encounter the Savior who is.
Not merely because sharing helps this ministry reach more people—although it genuinely does.
Someone may believe sexual sin has disqualified them forever.
Someone may think addiction has written the last sentence.
Someone may be one secret away from giving up.
Someone may have spent years believing church is only for people with clean histories.
Put Rahab's story in front of them.
Send this privately to the person who would never admit publicly that they need it.
But understand why.
You cannot buy grace.
And we will not tell you that giving money to us is a requirement for glorifying God.
It isn't.
God is glorified through lives surrendered to Jesus Christ.

But Scripture does teach voluntary, generous support for Gospel work. Paul wrote that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive their living from the Gospel, while Christian giving is to come from the heart rather than manipulation or compulsion.
Keep teaching.
Keep reaching.
Keep pointing wounded people away from hopelessness and toward Jesus Christ.
Sometimes the support you can give today is financial. Sometimes it is sharing. Sometimes it is prayer. Sometimes it is all three.
And there is more available even if you never spend a cent.
Invite your family.
Invite your friends.
Invite the believer who is struggling.
Invite the person who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker with uncomfortable questions.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing to say to someone with their history.
Because Rahab's story says otherwise.
And ultimately, Rahab's story is not powerful because Rahab was impressive.
It is powerful because God is merciful.
The Bible did not need to hide her past to demonstrate her faith.
Hebrews could say both.
Rahab.
The prostitute.
By faith.
Perhaps that is the sentence someone needed tonight.
Your worst chapter may be true.
But it does not have to become your final chapter.
Your sin may be real.
Your consequences may be real.
Your wounds may be real.
Your shame may feel real enough to suffocate you.
But Jesus Christ is real too.
His cross is real.
His resurrection is real.
His call to repentance is real.
His forgiveness is real.
His grace is real.
And transformation in Him is real.
Rahab entered Scripture carrying a label.
She entered Hebrews remembered for faith.
She entered the genealogy of Matthew on the road that leads the reader toward Christ.
That does not mean God promises every believer earthly prominence.
It means something better:
No repentant sinner who comes to Christ has to remain imprisoned by the identity sin once gave them.
So come out from behind the wall.
Stop negotiating with the darkness.
Stop rehearsing the prosecution's case as though Calvary never happened.
Confess what must be confessed.
Repent of what must be abandoned.
Make restitution where wisdom and righteousness require it.
Seek help where you need help.
Forgive where Christ calls you to forgive.
Ask forgiveness where you have wounded others.
And place your faith not in your ability to repair yourself, but in Jesus Christ.
Then walk.
One trembling step at a time.
Because the Gospel has never been about pretending there was no scandal.
It is about what Jesus Christ can do with sinners who surrender to Him.
So when your past whispers its old name tonight…
remember Rahab.
Remember Jericho.
Remember the woman in the window.
Remember the faith that acted.
Remember the mercy that rescued.
Remember the genealogy.
Remember Hebrews.
And above all…
remember Jesus.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Four words.
One testimony.
And perhaps the beginning of another person's courage to come home.
Because when Jesus takes hold of a surrendered life, the name shame gave you no longer gets to write the ending.
